definition.text: Scalability is the property of a system to handle a growing amount of work.

facts.text: A system is scalable when it can take on more work, typically by adding resources, without losing performance.
A package delivery system scales by adding vehicles, but a single warehouse that every package must pass through for sorting limits how far it can scale.
A search engine is a computing example: it must support growing numbers of users and growing numbers of indexed topics.
Marc Brooker defines a system as scalable in the range where the marginal cost of additional workload is nearly constant.
Scalability also depends on strategy: a system must repeatedly apply a cost-effective way of scaling, and it is hard to scale past the point where that strategy stops being financially viable.
Early Gnutella flooded every query to all nodes, so each peer's load grew with the number of peers; BitTorrent scales well because each peer's demand is independent of the number of peers.
A scalable database or transaction processing system can be upgraded with more processors, devices and storage to process more transactions, easily and without shutting down.

definition.text: Scalability can be measured along several dimensions, such as administrative, functional, geographic, load, generation and heterogeneous scalability.

facts.text: Administrative scalability is the ability of a growing number of organizations or users to access a system; geographic scalability is staying effective while expanding from a local area to a larger region.
Functional scalability is the ability to add new functionality without disrupting existing activities.
Load scalability is the ability of a distributed system to expand and contract for heavier or lighter loads, including how easily components can be modified, added or removed.
Generation scalability is scaling by adopting new generations of components; heterogeneous scalability is adopting components from different vendors.

title: Horizontal and vertical scaling
article: Scalability#Horizontal (scale out) and vertical scaling (scale up)

definition.text: Scaling horizontally (out) means adding nodes, while scaling vertically (up) means adding resources such as CPUs, memory or storage to a single node.

facts.text: Scaling out or in adds or removes nodes, such as adding a computer to a distributed application; an example is scaling out from one web server to three.
Scaling up or down adds resources to, or removes them from, a single node, typically CPUs, memory or storage in one computer.
Scale-out lets high-performance computing do tasks that once needed expensive supercomputers, and large social networks exceed the capacity of even the largest supercomputer.
Exploiting horizontal scalability requires software for efficient resource management and maintenance.

Scale-up avoids the management complexity, the more sophisticated programming to allocate tasks, and the throughput, latency and synchronization issues of spreading work across nodes, but some applications do not scale horizontally.

Vertical scaling adds power to an existing machine and is simple to implement, easier to manage and data consistent, but it risks high downtime, is harder to upgrade and can be a single point of failure.

Horizontal scaling adds more instances to the existing pool of servers so load is distributed more evenly, and brings more redundancy, better fault tolerance, flexibility and efficiency, and easier upgrades.
The costs of horizontal scaling are increased complexity, data inconsistency and increased load on downstream services.

definition.text: Eight common strategies for scaling a system are stateless services, horizontal scaling, load balancing, auto scaling, caching, database replication, database sharding and async processing.

facts.text: Stateless services do not rely on server-specific data, so they are easier to scale.
Horizontal scaling adds more servers so the workload can be shared, and a load balancer distributes incoming requests evenly across them.
Auto scaling policies adjust resources based on real-time traffic.
Caching reduces the load on the database and handles repetitive requests at scale.
Database replication copies data across multiple nodes to scale reads while improving redundancy; sharding distributes data across multiple instances to scale writes as well as reads.
Async processing moves time-consuming, resource-intensive tasks to background workers, and event-driven processing handles long-running tasks asynchronously, so the system can accept new requests.

definition.text: A scalability bottleneck is a part of the design, such as a centralized, slow or tightly coupled component, that stops a system from growing.

facts.text: A centralized component is one of three main bottlenecks to scalability and can become a single point of failure.
High-latency components, which perform time-consuming operations, are a second main bottleneck to scalability.
Tight coupling is the third main bottleneck because it makes components difficult to scale.
To build a scalable system, follow the principles of statelessness, loose coupling and asynchronous processing.

title: Database scaling strategies

definition.text: Database scalability is the ability of a database system to perform additional work when given greater hardware resources, such as more servers, processors, memory and storage.

facts.text: Algorithmic innovations for database scalability include row-level locking and table and index partitioning; architectural ones include shared-nothing and shared-everything designs for multi-server configurations.
Check the application's query patterns and create the right indexes, then pre-compute complex query results in materialized views to read them faster.
Denormalization reduces complex joins to improve query performance.
Vertical scaling boosts the database server with more CPU, RAM or storage, and caching frequently accessed data in a faster storage layer reduces database load.
Replicas of the primary database on other servers scale reads; sharding splits tables into smaller pieces spread across servers and scales writes as well as reads.

notes: ByteByteGo's seven-strategy guide is the main source of the list; the Wikipedia section supplies the definition and the two kinds of innovation.

definition.text: Adding processors speeds up a task less and less when part of the work is sequential, as Amdahl's law shows.

facts.text: System design is often advised to favor hardware scalability over per-node capacity, because adding a node is typically cheaper than performance tuning to raise what each node can handle.
Amdahl's law bounds the maximum speedup from P processors using α, the sequential fraction of a calculation; the remaining 1−α can be parallelized.
If 70% of a program can be parallelized, doubling the computing power from 4 to 8 processors speeds it up only by roughly one-fifth; a fully parallelizable problem would speed up twofold.
Adding more hardware is therefore not necessarily the optimal approach, because it has diminishing returns.

definition.text: The Universal Scalability Law models and optimizes the scalability of a distributed system using parameters such as contention and coherency.

facts.text: Neil J. Gunther coined the Universal Scalability Law, which quantifies scalability from contention and coherency.
Contention is delay from waiting or queueing for shared resources; coherence is delay for data to become consistent.
High contention indicates sequential processing that could be parallelized, while high coherency suggests excessive dependencies among processes, so interactions should be minimized.
The law lets you calculate in advance the maximum effective capacity of a system; scaling up beyond that point is a waste.

definition.text: In scale-out data storage, scalability is the largest cluster size that still guarantees full consistency, meaning only one valid version of the stored data in the whole cluster.

facts.text: Clusters that update copies asynchronously give 'lazy' redundancy and are called eventually consistent.

Eventual consistency suits designs that rate availability and responsiveness above consistency, such as web file-hosting services or web caches, and should be avoided for classical transaction-oriented applications.
In such clusters writes invalidate other copies but often do not wait for acknowledgements, and reads typically do not check every copy, so a read can miss the preceding write.
Many open-source and commercial scale-out storage clusters on standard PC hardware provide only eventual consistency, as some NoSQL databases such as CouchDB do.

definition.text: High availability is a characteristic of a system that aims to ensure an agreed level of operational performance, usually uptime, for a higher than normal period.

facts.text: Availability is the ability of a user to access a system to submit, update or retrieve work; if a user cannot access it, it is unavailable from the user's perspective.
Reliability engineering offers three design principles for high availability: eliminate single points of failure, provide reliable crossover, and detect failures as they occur.
Eliminating single points of failure means building in redundancy so that the failure of a component does not mean the failure of the entire system.
In redundant systems the crossover point itself tends to become a single point of failure, so reliable systems must provide for reliable crossover.

Adding components can undermine availability because complex systems have more potential failure points, but one simple machine must be taken down entirely for patching and operating system upgrades; advanced designs use load balancing and failover instead.
The most common cause of outages is human error, so high availability in complex systems requires less human intervention to restore operation.
A reliable system is available, but an available system is not necessarily reliable: high reliability contributes to high availability, yet a system can be highly available even if it is unreliable.

A fault-tolerant system has no service interruption but a significantly higher cost, while a highly available system has minimal interruption; fault tolerance needs full hardware redundancy so a second system takes over with no loss in uptime.

title: Availability and the nines

definition.text: Availability is the percentage of time a system is up, usually measured over a year and often quoted in nines.

facts.text: Availability is quoted in nines: 90% availability is one nine, 99% is two nines, 99.9% is three nines, and so on.
As the number of nines grows, the availability target becomes exponentially more stringent.
Per year, 99.9% availability allows about 9 hours of downtime, 99.99% about 53 minutes and 99.999% about 5.3 minutes.
A mnemonic says five nines allows approximately 5 minutes of downtime per year; multiply or divide by 10 for other levels, so four nines is 50 minutes and six nines is 0.5 minutes.
Service level agreements often state monthly downtime or availability so service credits can match monthly billing cycles.
Uptime and availability are not always the same: a system can be up while its service is not available, as in a network outage.
Availability is the time a system remains operational to perform its required function in a specific period, often quantified as uptime or downtime as a percentage of time the service is available.
Availability equals uptime divided by the sum of uptime and downtime, and is generally measured in the number of 9s.

notes: The Wikipedia table gives rounded yearly figures (9 hours, 53 minutes, 5.3 minutes); Singh's table gives 8.77 hours, 52.6 minutes and 5.25 minutes for the same levels, which is rounding, not a conflict.

definition.text: Measured availability depends on interpretation, because what users experience can differ from the uptime an administrator reports.

facts.text: A system up all year can still be hit by a 9-hour network failure at peak usage: users see it as unavailable while the administrator claims 100% uptime.
By the true definition of availability, that system is approximately 99.9% available, or three nines: 8751 hours of available time out of 8760 hours.

Users often deem a system with performance problems partly or wholly unavailable even while it functions, and unavailable application functions may go unnoticed by administrators, so a true availability measure is holistic.
Availability must be measured with comprehensive monitoring tools that are themselves highly available.

definition.text: Downtime is a period when a system is unavailable, and it is either scheduled, usually for maintenance, or unscheduled, usually from a failure.

facts.text: Scheduled downtime typically comes from disruptive maintenance, such as patches or configuration changes that need a reboot, and is a logical, management-initiated event.
Unscheduled downtime typically arises from a physical event such as a hardware or software failure, power outage, over-temperature shutdown or severed network connection.
Many sites exclude scheduled downtime from availability calculations and so claim very high availability, but for true high availability downtime is downtime whether or not it is scheduled.

Truly continuous availability is rare and costly: specialty designs remove every single point of failure and allow online upgrades, patches and replacements of hardware, network, operating system, middleware and applications.

title: Recovery time and recovery point objectives

definition.text: Recovery time, or recovery time objective, is the total time needed to recover fully from an outage and is closely related to availability.

facts.text: Recovery time, also called recovery time objective (RTO) or estimated time of repair, is the time for a planned outage or for full recovery from an unplanned one; mean time to recovery (MTTR) is another metric.
Recovery time can be infinite, for example when a fire or flood destroys a data center and there is no secondary disaster recovery data center.
The Recovery Point Objective sets the acceptable data loss for various failure events, a concern separate from data availability, which is how faithfully databases record and report transactions.
Some users can tolerate service interruptions but not data loss, and a service level agreement formalizes an organization's availability objectives and requirements.

title: Redundancy

definition.text: Redundancy is the intentional duplication of critical components or functions of a system to raise its reliability, usually as a backup or fail-safe.

facts.text: Passive redundancy uses excess capacity to reduce the impact of component failures, accepting some performance decline when a limited number of failures occur.
Active redundancy runs multiple items of the same kind and monitors them; voting logic linked to switching reconfigures around a failed item automatically, so performance does not decline.

The simplest voting logic pairs a primary with an alternate running similar software; the alternate's output stays inactive until the primary's activity message stops, then it takes over after a brief delay.

With an odd number of three or more devices doing identical work, voting logic compares the outputs and the majority overrides any disagreeing device, so a single fault does not interrupt operation (triple modular redundancy).
For N parallel components of availability X, combined availability is 1 - (1 - X)^N, so redundancy raises it exponentially: ten hosts with only 50% availability each reach 99.9023%.
The formula holds only if failures are independent, for example copies not in the same data center, and failures can be detected; two power supplies on one socket fail together.

Redundancy does not always raise availability, because it adds complexity. Marc Brooker advises ensuring a net-positive gain, independent failures, reliable detection of healthy components, and reliable scale-out and scale-in.
Active redundancy adds failure modes of its own: errors in voting logic can leave both outputs active or inactive, or make outputs flutter on and off, as in continuous reconfiguration.

title: Availability in sequence and in parallel

definition.text: Components in sequence multiply their availabilities and so lower the total, while components in parallel raise the total.

facts.text: A service made of failure-prone components has an overall availability that depends on whether the components are in sequence or in parallel.
In sequence, total availability is the product of the components' availabilities, so it decreases: two components at 99.9% each give 99.8%.
In parallel, total availability is 1 minus the product of the components' unavailabilities, so it increases: two components at 99.9% each give 99.9999%.

definition.text: A computer cluster is a group of two or more computers, or nodes, that run in parallel to achieve a common goal.

facts.text: A cluster distributes workloads of many parallelizable tasks among its nodes, so the tasks use the combined memory and processing power of every computer to raise overall performance.
Nodes are connected by a network for internode communication and joined into a cluster by software; the cluster may have shared storage, local storage on each node, or both.
Typically at least one node is the leader node and entry point, delegating incoming work to other nodes and, if needed, aggregating results into a response for the user.
Ideally a cluster functions as a single system that users cannot tell from one machine, and it is designed to minimize latency and prevent bottlenecks in node-to-node communication.
Clusters are generally of three types: highly available or fail-over, load balancing, and high-performance computing.
Four key advantages of clustering are high availability, scalability, performance and cost-effectiveness.

Clustering adds complexity: the operating system, application and dependencies must be installed and updated on every node, usage monitored, logs aggregated, and shared storage and distributed data kept safe and in sync.
Many technologies offer a clustering mode, such as Kubernetes and Amazon ECS for containers, Cassandra and MongoDB for databases, and Redis for caches.

definition.text: The two most common high availability clustering configurations are active-active and active-passive.

facts.text: An active-active cluster has at least two nodes all running the same kind of service simultaneously; its main purpose is load balancing, with a load balancer spreading work so no node is overloaded.
Because more nodes are available to serve, an active-active cluster improves throughput and response times.
An active-passive cluster also has at least two nodes, but not all are active: with two nodes, if the first is active the second must be passive or on standby.

definition.text: Clustering links servers that work together toward a common purpose, while load balancing spreads requests across servers that are unaware of each other.

facts.text: Load balancing shares traits with clustering but is a different process; clustering provides redundancy and boosts capacity and availability.
Servers in a cluster are aware of each other, whereas servers behind a load balancer are not and simply react to the requests it sends them.
Load balancing can be used together with clustering, and also with independent servers that share a purpose such as running a website, business application or web service.

title: Autoscaling

definition.text: Autoscaling is a cloud computing method that automatically adjusts the number of active servers in a server farm to match the load on the farm.

facts.text: Autoscaling launches servers when activity is high and removes them when it is low, so a farm runs just enough servers for the current load while still absorbing sudden, large spikes.

Because it follows actual usage instead of a fixed daily or weekly schedule, autoscaling handles unexpected traffic spikes better, and in the cloud it can lower bills because providers charge for usage, not peak capacity.

A health check tells the group whether an instance exists and is reachable, or is in service with its load balancer; unhealthy instances are replaced automatically, which also protects against hardware, network and application failures.

An autoscaling group is the set of instances under autoscaling. Its desired capacity is how many instances it should have, never below the minimum size or above the maximum size; it launches or removes instances to match.
A scaling policy changes the desired capacity when a metric such as CPU utilization, memory or network usage crosses a threshold; a cooldown period blocks further scaling actions right after one.

Autoscaling is reactive by default, scaling only in response to real-time metrics, which is insufficient when load changes very quickly. Scheduled scaling changes the size limits or desired capacity at set times for known, sudden changes.

Predictive autoscaling combines recent usage trends with historical data to forecast demand and scale ahead of it; Netflix found its predictive engine Scryer gave better results than Amazon's reactive autoscaling for some workloads.
Netflix found that aggressive scaling up, with delayed and cautious scaling down, served its goals of uptime and responsiveness best.

title: Mean time between failures

definition.text: Mean time between failures (MTBF) is the predicted average time between inherent failures of a repairable system during normal operation.

facts.text: MTBF is the average time between failures of a repairable system in normal operation; for a non-repairable system the equivalent measure is mean time to failure (MTTF).
For example, three identical systems that fail after 100, 120 and 130 hours have an MTBF of 116.667 hours, the average of the three failure times.
What counts as a failure sets the MTBF: failures put the system out of service for repair, while faults that can be left unrepaired and units down for scheduled maintenance are not counted.
MTBF calculations assume the system is in its useful life with a constant failure rate, which makes MTBF the reciprocal of the failure rate; the chance of surviving a duration T is then exp(-T/MTBF).
A system survives to its MTBF with probability 1/e, about 37%, not the 50% many engineers assume; that misreading can lead to bad design decisions.
Two components in series fail the system if either fails, giving an MTBF of 1/(1/MTBF1 + 1/MTBF2), so adding components in series lowers the MTBF.

Two components in parallel fail the system only if the second fails while the first is under repair, so the MTBF depends on mean down time: the faster the repair, the smaller the vulnerability window.
MTBF serves as a reliability parameter and for comparing systems or designs, but it is only a mean lifetime; for disk drives, the annualized failure rate is usually more relevant than MTBF.

notes: The manufacturing (total productive maintenance) and censored-data sections were skipped as outside system design; the 'series' fact states the formula that sentence 963bc9a4fda5 gives only as garbled math, 1/(1/m1+1/m2).

definition.text: Mean time to repair (MTTR) is the average time needed to repair a failed component or device, a basic measure of how maintainable a repairable item is.

facts.text: MTTR is the total corrective maintenance time for failures divided by the number of corrective maintenance actions in a period; it generally excludes lead time for parts and other administrative or logistic downtime.

In fault-tolerant design MTTR also counts the time a fault stays latent, from failure until detection; if a latent fault goes unnoticed until an independent failure, the system may be unable to recover.

Mean time to recovery runs from discovering a failure to resuming operation; mean time to repair runs only from when repairs begin. A 24-hour repair promise with 6 days of added delays is no better than a 7-day recovery promise.
With equal MTBF, a 24-hour MTTR gives higher operational availability than a 7-day one. With a backup, the MTBF must be long enough to repair a failed device before the backup fails too.

definition.text: Computing uses hardware, information, time and software redundancy, plus dissimilar and geographic variants, to keep a system running when parts fail.

facts.text: Computing has four major forms of redundancy: hardware (dual or triple modular), information (error detection and correction), time (repeating an operation or sending several copies of data) and software (N-version programming).

Dissimilar redundancy uses different things instead of copies of the same thing, because different things are unlikely to share identical flaws; it is common for software, since identical software contains identical flaws.
Geographic redundancy separates backup devices so that power outages, floods, fires or storms are less likely to disable most or all of the system.

Cloud providers such as AWS, Google Cloud Platform and Azure use it for high availability and fault tolerance; separation ranges from over 621 miles (999 km) down to buildings over 300 feet (91 m) apart on one campus.

title: Amdahl's law

definition.text: Amdahl's law is a formula that limits the speedup of a task as resources are added to the system executing it.

facts.text: The overall gain from optimizing one part of a system is limited by the fraction of time that part is actually used, which caps the speedup from adding resources.

In parallel computing it predicts the theoretical speedup from multiple processors; the part that cannot run in parallel, such as building a file list before threads process the files, sets the limit.
Overall speedup is 1 divided by the sum of the unimproved share of the time and the improved share divided by its speedup factor, so it is often much lower than expected.
Speeding up a part that takes 10% of execution time by a factor of 10,000 gives an overall speedup of only 1.11, an 11% improvement.
Optimizing a section that takes 99% of the time by a factor of 100 gives an overall speedup of only 50: half the potential gain is lost to the remaining 1%.
Improve the part that takes most time: with parts of 3 s and 1 s, making the 3 s part twice as fast gives 1.60 overall, but making the 1 s part five times faster gives only 1.25.

For a fixed-size computation each added processor adds less usable power than the last, with throughput heading toward 1/(1-p), p being the parallel share; memory and I/O bandwidth that do not scale lower returns further.

notes: Extends the existing 'Diminishing returns of adding hardware' entry, which cites only the Amdahl example inside the Scalability article; the 1/(1-p) limit is the sentence's garbled '11-p'.

title: Capacity planning

definition.text: Capacity planning is the process of determining the capacity needed to meet changing demand; in IT it estimates the storage, hardware, software and connection resources required over a future period.

facts.text: IT capacity planning estimates the storage, hardware, software and connection resources needed over a future period, so a system can handle more users or interactions.
A mismatch between capacity and demand leaves resources under-utilized or demand unmet; the goal of capacity planning is to minimize this gap.

Capacity strategies are lead (add capacity as demand grows), lag (add only when running at full capacity), match (add small amounts as demand changes) and adjustment; lead is risky when demand is unpredictable, lag can lose users.

The SRE book advises pairing capacity planning with performance testing to find the load at which the service fails; planning lowers the chance of cascading failure but cannot prevent it after large infrastructure losses.

notes: Wikipedia's page is mostly about manufacturing capacity (OEE, shifts, workers); only the IT lines and the strategy names were used, with the SRE book supplying the engineering advice.

title: Stateless and stateful services

definition.text: A stateless protocol is one where the receiver keeps no session state from previous requests, while a stateful protocol may retain it.

facts.text: In a stateless protocol the sender supplies the relevant session state so each request can be understood in isolation; in a stateful protocol the receiver may retain session state from earlier requests.

IP and HTTP are stateless; TCP and FTP are stateful. An FTP server keeps the user's authentication, working directory and transfer mode as session state, while an HTTP server understands each request alone.

Stateless protocols have better visibility, reliability and scalability: monitoring needs only one request, recovery from failures such as packet loss is easier, and the server can quickly free resources because it stores no session state.
The cost is performance: repetitive data is sent with every request because the receiver does not retain or reuse it.
HTTP servers add state with a session identifier in a cookie that refers to session state stored on the server, effectively building a stateful protocol on top of HTTP.
Stateless and stateful protocols stack in layers: stateless HTTP runs over stateful TCP, which runs over stateless IP.
Stateless web servers can be autoscaled. Scaling stateless applications on Kubernetes only means adding more pods, but stateful workloads are harder because their state must survive a pod restart.

notes: Titled for the interview concept (stateless versus stateful services); the Wikipedia page is about protocols, so the server-side scaling fact comes from the primer and Kubernetes sentences.
